 One Nation, One Election: The Road Ahead 
 Tags: GS Paper - 2 
 Federalism 
 Co-operative Federalism 
 Constitutional Amendments 
 Centre-State Relations 
 This editorial is based on " India's election calendar needs a reset " published in the Economic Times on 14/11/2026. The article highlights that simultaneous elections can boost administrative efficiency and capital spending, provided federal consensus, constructive confidence votes, and legal limits on poll deferrals safeguard democracy. 
 For Prelims: One Nation, One Election , Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024 , Lok Sabha , Law Commission , NITI Aayog , Electoral Photo Identity Card , Election Commission , Article 327 , Joint Parliamentary Committee , Model Code of Conduct , Right to Education Act, 2009 , Federalism , Basic Structure , President , Governor , Parliament , Vote of No Confidence . 
 For Mains: Key facts regarding One Nation One Election, Arguments in favour and arguments against ONOE, Measures needed to implement ONOE in India. 
 One Nation, One Election (ONOE) aims to synchronise Lok Sabha and State Assembly polls to end perpetual campaign mode and policy paralysis. Supported by the Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024 , it promises administrative efficiency, lower recurring costs, and capital-expenditure focus. However, critics warn of federal erosion, electoral coattail effects , and short-lived replacement legislatures. Realising this reform requires federal consensus and robust constitutional safeguards.    
 What is One Nation One Election?   
 About: ONOE refers to synchronising elections to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies within a common electoral cycle.    
 Electors would cast separate votes for their MP and MLA , while polling could occur in multiple phases across India.    
 Its principal objectives are to reduce recurring electoral expenditure , repeated administrative deployment and election-related disruption, while improving policy continuity and administrative efficiency .   
 Evolution of Simultaneous Elections: India broadly followed simultaneous parliamentary and Assembly elections during 1951–52, 1957, 1962 and 1967 .    
 The cycle fragmented after the premature dissolution of some Assemblies in 1968–69 and the Lok Sabha in 1970 .    
 Partial synchronisation continues. Andhra Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Odisha and Sikkim held Assembly elections alongside the 2024 Lok Sabha election , demonstrating the operational practice of conducting both elections together.   
 Commission and Committee Recommendations: The Law Commission ’s 170 th Report, 1999 , favoured holding Lok Sabha and Assembly elections together once every five years.    
 The Parliamentary Standing Committee’s 79 th Report, 2015 , examined feasibility and suggested a phased approach to synchronisation, emphasising the need for political agreement.    
 A 2017 NITI Aayog Discussion paper proposed a "phase-wise" synchronisation strategy explicitly designed to minimise constitutional disruption.   
 Subsequently, the Law Commission’s 2018 Draft Report examined constitutional questions and mechanisms for addressing situations such as a hung legislature .    
 High-Level Committee Recommendations: The Ram Nath Kovind-led High-Level Committee , which submitted its report in March 2024 , recommended a two-step framework :    
 First, simultaneous Lok Sabha and Assembly elections; second, Panchayat and Municipal elections within 100 days of those elections.    
 It also recommended a single electoral roll and common Electoral Photo Identity Card , prepared by the Election Commission in consultation with State Election Commissions.    
 The Committee envisaged advance planning for personnel, security forces and voting equipment. The Union Cabinet accepted its recommendations in September 2024.   
 Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024: The Bill proposes inserting Article 82A (simultaneous elections to the Lok Sabha and all Legislative Assemblies) and amending Article 83 (duration of Houses of Parliament), Article 172 (duration of State Legislatures) and Article 327 (Parliament’s power to make provisions relating to elections to legislatures).    
 A presidential notification issued on the first sitting of the Lok Sabha after a general election would establish an “appointed date” ; Assemblies elected subsequently would have their terms aligned with that Lok Sabha’s expiry.    
 Following premature dissolution, the replacement legislature would serve the unexpired term .    
 The Bill also permits the President, on the Election Commission’s recommendation, to defer a particular Assembly election while retaining its common expiry date.    
 Its provisions concern parliamentary and Assembly elections ; local-body synchronisation and the common electoral roll remain separate recommendations.     
 Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2024: This accompanying Bill seeks to extend electoral synchronisation to the Assemblies of Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir .    
 It proposes consequential amendments to the Government of Union Territories Act, 1963 , the Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi Act, 1991 , and the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 .    
 Its purpose is to align these UT Assemblies with the proposed common electoral cycle.     
 Present Status and Constitutional Considerations: As of November 2026, the two Bills remain under Joint Parliamentary Committee examination , and nationwide ONOE has not been implemented.    
 Parliamentary scrutiny encompasses federalism, legislative tenure, democratic accountability and Election Commission powers .    
 Separately, the High-Level Committee recommended ratification by at least half the states for constitutional changes concerning local-body synchronisation and the common electoral roll.    
 What are Arguments in Favour of One Nation, One Election (ONOE)?   
 Lower Recurring Election Costs and Better Resource Utilisation: ONOE could generate economies of scale by combining expenditure on polling premises, transport, training, communication and election management.    
 The 2024 Lok Sabha election involved 10,52,664 polling stations , illustrating the extensive infrastructure mobilised for a national electoral exercise.    
 Conducting Assembly polls alongside parliamentary polls could reduce repeated mobilisation of these facilities.     
 Fewer Repeated Restrictions Under the Model Code of Conduct: Synchronised elections could provide longer periods for fresh project approvals, policy announcements and administrative decisions between electoral cycles.    
 During the 2024 general election , the Model Code of Conduct (MCC) operated from the election announcement in March until its withdrawal on 6 th June 2024 . Repeated, separate elections create additional periods of election-related restrictions in the jurisdictions concerned.    
 ONOE could therefore improve implementation continuity , particularly for projects requiring fresh sanctions, while recognising that the MCC already permits many ongoing works and essential services.     
 Reduced Diversion of Administrative and Security Capacity: A combined electoral exercise could reduce repeated requisitioning, training and movement of district officials, police personnel and security forces , allowing greater attention to routine administration and public safety between elections.    
 Official information on the 2024 general election recorded mobilisation of approximately 1.5 crore polling and security personnel . This scale demonstrates the opportunity cost of electoral deployment .    
 Synchronisation could consolidate assignments and reduce repeated disruption to activities such as revenue administration, grievance redressal and regular policing.     
 Greater Protection of Teaching Time and School Functioning: ONOE could reduce recurring interruptions caused by teachers’ polling assignments, election training and the use of school premises .    
 In a March 2026 parliamentary reply, the Ministry of Education reiterated that Section 27 of the Right to Education Act, 2009 , permits teachers’ deployment for election duties, while stressing safeguards against disruption to learning.    
 Consolidating poll-related assignments could help protect instructional continuity , especially in schools with limited staff, and make the academic calendar easier to plan around election requirements.     
 Stronger Orientation Towards Capital Expenditure: Supporters argue that a common electoral cycle could create greater space for long-term infrastructure investment , as governments face fewer overlapping election deadlines.    
 A 2025 working paper found that simultaneous-election episodes were associated with a higher capital-to-current expenditure ratio .    
 This supports an argument about the quality of public expenditure . Governments may have greater scope to prioritise assets such as roads, irrigation and public infrastructure.     
 Lower Electoral Uncertainty and Potential Economic Gains: Coordinating elections could reduce repeated periods of uncertainty surrounding policy priorities, government formation and investment decisions.    
 The same August 2025 working paper , examining India’s electoral experience over 1952–2023 , estimated a national-level growth differential of approximately 1.5 percentage points around simultaneous-election episodes compared with staggered episodes.    
 This provides research support for examining ONOE as an economic coordination reform .     
 Lower Participation Costs for Migrant and Working Voters: Simultaneous voting could reduce the number of journeys, leave applications and workdays required to participate in parliamentary and Assembly elections.    
 The Election Commission has identified migration-related inability to vote as an important obstacle to electoral participation. For example, a worker registered in their home constituency could cast both votes during one return visit , reducing travel expenditure and foregone earnings.    
 This strengthens the argument for voter convenience and inclusive participation .     
 Reduced Repetition of Campaign Expenditure and Fundraising: A common election period could allow parties to share spending on campaign offices, publicity, travel and organisational mobilisation across parliamentary and Assembly contests.    
 An ADR-reported analysis of regional parties’ 2024–25 accounts found that 15 regional parties spent over 55% of their total expenditure on elections , demonstrating the financial importance of campaigning.    
 What are Arguments Against One Nation, One Election (ONOE)?   
 Erosion of Federal Autonomy and State Electoral Mandates: Critics argue that aligning Assembly tenures with the Lok Sabha makes state electoral calendars dependent on a Union-level institution , despite states possessing distinct constitutional responsibilities and political mandates.    
 The constitutional concern draws on S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) , which recognised federalism as part of the Basic Structure .    
 Administrative convenience therefore needs to be weighed against the autonomy of state-level representative institutions.     
 Dilution of Regional Issues Through Electoral Coattail Effects: Simultaneous campaigns could increase the influence of party branding, national leadership and national narratives over assessments of individual candidates and state-specific concerns.    
 A 2025 peer-reviewed study in the Journal of Comparative Economics found a 21% higher probability of the same party winning across parliamentary and Assembly tiers under synchronised elections. This supports concerns about straight-ticket voting and party salience .     
 Fewer Opportunities for Interim Electoral Accountability: Staggered elections provide periodic opportunities for citizens to communicate dissatisfaction, test competing political programmes and influence national political debate between general elections.    
 Synchronisation would concentrate these opportunities into a common cycle, potentially weakening continuous electoral feedback .   
 For example, Delhi’s February 2025 Assembly election , covering 70 seats , provided a separate occasion to evaluate the territorial administration after the parliamentary election.    
 Critics value such independently timed contests as instruments of issue-specific accountability , while recognising that legislative scrutiny and other accountability mechanisms would continue.     
 Short-Lived Legislatures and Repeated Mid-Term Elections: Parliamentary governments can fall through coalition breakdowns or loss of legislative confidence, so synchronisation cannot ensure political stability.    
 Under the proposed framework, a replacement legislature elected near the common cycle’s end could receive an extremely short tenure.    
 For instance, a fresh Assembly elected with eight months remaining would soon face another election, limiting time for budgeting, legislative work and policy implementation.    
 PRS Legislative Research’s June 2025 assessment specifically warns that some legislatures could have terms of less than one year , undermining effective governance.     
 Open-Ended Election Deferrals and Governance Uncertainty: The proposed power to defer an Assembly election raises concerns about institutional discretion, electoral certainty and continuity of representative government .    
 PRS identifies that the Bill specifies neither detailed grounds nor an outer time limit for postponement.    
 If an Assembly’s term expires before the delayed election, the proposal also leaves unclear who would govern during the intervening period and under what authority.    
 This creates potential disputes involving the Election Commission, President , Governor and Parliament , making explicit safeguards essential.     
 Concentrated Logistical Demands and Reduced Scheduling Flexibility: ONOE could reduce repeated mobilisation while increasing the capacity required during a common electoral period.    
 Security deployment, reserve equipment, counting arrangements and trained personnel would need to accommodate parliamentary and Assembly contests together.    
 The scheduling challenge is illustrated by West Bengal’s 2024 parliamentary polling across all 7 phases . Even with phased simultaneous elections, synchronisation could constrain flexibility to accommodate regional weather conditions, festivals, security requirements and unexpected disruptions across different states.     
 Uncertain Net Savings and Substantial Equipment Lifecycle Costs: Critics question whether operational savings would outweigh expenditure on procurement, storage, maintenance, replacement and reserve voting equipment .    
 An ECI estimate reported in January 2024 , based on its communication to the Law Ministry, placed new EVM procurement requirements under simultaneous elections at approximately ₹10,000 crore every 15 years .    
 Moreover, synchronising dates would leave the underlying incentives for expensive candidate campaigns and competitive political fundraising largely intact.     
 Persistence of Political Business Cycles and Strategic Service Delivery: Synchronisation may concentrate election-driven incentives instead of eliminating them, potentially encouraging governments to time visible benefits around a high-stakes national electoral window.    
 A September 2025 working paper , Between the Ballots , found sharper fluctuations in electricity provision around concurrent elections, using nighttime luminosity as a proxy : declines before elections were followed by a surge during the election month.    
 These findings challenge the assumption that ONOE would automatically produce fiscal discipline or stable public-service delivery , and highlight the continuing importance of institutional checks on electoral opportunism.   
 What Measures Need to be Adopted to Implement One Nation, One Election in India?   
 Build a Federal Consensus Through a Transparent Transition Agreement: Parliament should develop a negotiated transition framework with state governments, regional parties and constitutional experts before finalising synchronisation.    
 A publicly accessible state-wise tenure-impact statement should show how many months each Assembly would lose, the alternatives considered and the reasons for the chosen arrangement.    
 Constitutional and statutory amendments should follow the applicable procedures, including state ratification wherever required. This would translate cooperative federalism into a reviewable process and help prevent administrative convenience from overriding representative mandates.     
 Parliamentary Accountability Through Constructive Confidence Mechanisms: India should examine a constructive vote of no confidence , under which a legislature replaces an incumbent government by simultaneously demonstrating majority support for a successor. Article 67 of Germany’s Basic Law provides a comparative example.    
 Any Indian adaptation would require appropriate constitutional examination and safeguards against prolonged minority government.    
 A complementary time-bound government-formation procedure should establish deadlines for floor tests and alternative coalition formation, followed by elections when no viable majority emerges.     
 Place Clear Legal Limits on Election Deferrals: The legislation should specify permissible grounds, maximum postponement periods and a reasoned-order requirement for deferring an Assembly election.    
 Exceptional circumstances should trigger documented assessments, periodic review and access to expedited judicial scrutiny . The law should also clarify interim governance, caretaker powers and the constitutional conditions governing any resort to President’s Rule.    
 For example, a disaster-related postponement should carry a published reassessment date and a revised polling plan. These provisions would address the absence of explicit postponement limits and governance arrangements identified in PRS’s examination of the Bill.     
 Certify Operational Readiness Before Fixing the Common Polling Window: The Election Commission, state electoral authorities and security agencies should prepare a scenario-based logistics model covering personnel, equipment, transport, counting centres and disaster contingencies.    
 Districts should demonstrate readiness against published standards for reserve availability, replacement time and accessible polling capacity . Procurement and storage plans should follow independently assessed requirements, while existing First Level Checking and equipment randomisation should remain integral safeguards.    
 For instance, simulations should establish whether a failed machine can be replaced promptly in a remote constituency when neighbouring districts are simultaneously polling.     
 Create Interoperable Electoral Rolls With Protection Against Exclusion: If a common electoral roll is adopted, it should use shared data standards with clearly distributed verification responsibilities between the ECI and State Election Commissions.    
 Every correction should generate an auditable change history , showing its origin, verification and effect across electoral tiers. Automated duplicate detection should flag cases for examination; deletion decisions should retain notice, field verification and hearing safeguards.    
 A time-bound grievance system should prioritise migrants, newly eligible voters and persons with disabilities. This would combine administrative integration with due process, data protection and universal adult franchise .     
 Protect Independent Voter Choice and State-Specific Political Debate: The ECI should commission voter-comprehension trials to test whether electors can clearly distinguish parliamentary and Assembly contests under different polling-station layouts and information formats.    
 Civic education should explain the respective responsibilities of Union and state governments through multilingual, accessible and politically neutral material .    
 Public broadcasters could organise separate issue-based discussions for each electoral tier, with transparent participation rules. Implementation should preserve voters’ ability to assess candidates and governments independently.     
 Make Financial Savings Verifiable Through Lifecycle Budgeting: Governments should publish a full lifecycle cost assessment comparing synchronised and staggered elections over the same period.    
 It should include procurement, maintenance, warehousing, reserve equipment, personnel deployment and replacement costs, with a transparent Union–state cost-sharing framework .    
 CAG performance-audit principles—economy, efficiency and effectiveness—provide an appropriate framework for testing whether claimed savings translate into measurable public value.     
 Conclusion    
 Synchronising India’s electoral cycle offers tangible gains in administrative continuity , capital expenditure, and voter convenience, yet administrative efficiency cannot supersede constitutional federalism. As the Joint Parliamentary Committee scrutinises the 129 th Amendment Bill, Parliament must pair transition timelines with strict legal limits on election deferrals, constructive confidence mechanisms , and auditable electoral rolls . Only a consensus-driven, federally balanced framework can deliver durable electoral alignment without compromising democratic accountability.    
 Drishti Mains Question: 
 Examine the potential benefits of One Nation, One Election in reducing electoral expenditure and improving administrative efficiency in India.  
 Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)    
 1. What is One Nation, One Election?  
 It refers to synchronising elections to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies within a common electoral cycle, while voters cast separate votes for their MP and MLA.   
 2. Which constitutional provisions are proposed to be amended under the Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024?  
 The Bill proposes inserting Article 82A and amending Articles 83, 172 and 327 to facilitate simultaneous elections.   
 3. What were the key recommendations of the Ram Nath Kovind-led High-Level Committee?  
 It recommended a two-step framework: simultaneous Lok Sabha and Assembly elections, followed by local-body elections within 100 days. It also proposed a common electoral roll and EPIC.   
 4. What are the major concerns associated with ONOE?  
 Key concerns include erosion of federal autonomy, dilution of regional issues, reduced electoral accountability, short legislative tenures, logistical challenges and uncertainty surrounding election deferrals.   
 5. What is the present status of the ONOE proposals as of November 2026?  
 The Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024, and the accompanying Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2024, remain under Joint Parliamentary Committee examination; nationwide implementation has not taken place.   
 UPSC Civil Services Examination, Previous Year Questions (PYQs) 
 Prelims     
 Q. Consider the following statements: (2017) 
 The Election Commission of India is a five-member body.    
 Union Ministry of Home Affairs decides the election schedule for the conduct of both general elections and bye-elections.    
 Election Commission resolves the disputes relating to splits/mergers of recognised political parties.    
 Which of the statements given above is/are correct?   
 (a) 1 and 2 only    
 (b) 2 only    
 (c) 2 and 3 only    
 (d) 3 only    
 Ans: (d) 
 Mains     
 Q. Examine the need for electoral reforms as suggested by various committees with particular reference to “one nation - one election" principle. (2024) 
 Q. Discuss the role of the Election Commission of India in the light of the evolution of the Model Code of Conduct. (2022) 
 Q. Simultaneous election to the Lok Sabha and the State Assemblies will limit the amount of time and money spent in electioneering but it will reduce the government’s accountability to the people”. Discuss. (2017) 
 Q. To enhance the quality of democracy in India the Election Commission of India has proposed electoral reforms in 2016. What are the suggested reforms and how far are they significant to make democracy successful? (2017)
